scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a recommendation response that backs teaching ideas before facts while arguing the two must grow together; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Schools often ask students to memorise long lists of facts before they understand what those facts mean.
Some people recommend that educators should teach facts only after students have first studied the ideas, trends, and concepts that explain them.
I agree that understanding concepts first makes learning richer, but I believe facts and ideas must often be taught together rather than in a strict order.
First, learning the big ideas before the details helps facts make real sense.
When students grasp the concept behind a subject, isolated facts become far easier to understand and remember.
For example, a student who first understands why wars begin will remember the relevant dates and battles much more easily.
This shows that concepts give facts a framework, turning scattered information into genuine knowledge.
Teaching ideas first also makes a subject more interesting, since students see the purpose behind what they study.
Facts learned without understanding are quickly forgotten, while facts tied to ideas tend to last.
In this sense, beginning with concepts is a sound teaching principle.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why a strict order fails

sentences.text: Second, however, teaching facts only after concepts would be too rigid to follow in practice.
Many concepts simply cannot be understood without knowing at least some basic facts first.
Consider a child who cannot grasp the idea of multiplication without first learning the simple facts of counting and addition.
Such cases show that facts and ideas usually depend on each other and grow together.
A teacher who refused to mention any fact until every concept was mastered would slow learning to a crawl.
In reality, good teaching weaves facts and concepts together so that each one supports the other.
Rigid ordering, then, is far less useful than a flexible blend of the two.
In conclusion, students do understand facts more deeply when they first grasp the ideas behind them.
But teaching facts strictly after concepts ignores how closely the two are connected.
The best teaching introduces ideas and facts side by side, letting understanding and detail grow together.
